label: EMS, fire and hazardous materials response
description: The agencies that respond on the street: an EMS agency, a fire department, a hazardous materials team, technical rescue, the dispatch center as it sends those units, and the regional healthcare coalition on the hospital side of a mass casualty incident. Roles are grouped in teams (Command, Medical, Fire and rescue, Hazmat, Dispatch, Healthcare coalition) so an exercise can use the whole roster or only the teams it needs.

vocabulary.facility: the incident scene (the hot, warm and cold zones, the command post, the staging area and the treatment areas)
vocabulary.public: patients, bystanders, residents inside the protective action zone, families looking for relatives, and the receiving hospitals
vocabulary.frontline: paramedics and EMTs, firefighters, company officers, hazmat technicians, telecommunicators

it: computer-aided dispatch (CAD), mobile data terminals and automatic vehicle location
regional hospital capacity and patient tracking system
medical communications center and hospital status board
geographic information system, hydrant and pre-incident plan maps
records management and fire incident reporting
mass notification and alert systems used for protective actions
county network, email and the exercise-day laptops
ot: conventional, trunked and interoperability radio channels, and portable radios
multi-gas meters, photoionization detectors, radiation detectors and chemical identification instruments
plume modeling software and wind sensors
thermal imaging cameras and self-contained breathing apparatus
triage tags, wristbands and patient tracking equipment
apparatus pumps, aerial devices and water supply
structural monitoring and shoring for collapse

roles.name: Incident Commander
roles.description: Owns strategy, declares the incident type (including a mass casualty incident), transfers command with a briefing, and requests mutual aid and state resources.

roles.name: Safety Officer
roles.description: Watches the hazards and can stop unsafe acts: checks the hot, warm and cold zones and the PPE level set by the Hazmat Group, collapse and secondary-device concerns, rehab, and that personnel accountability is kept.

roles.name: Public Information Officer
roles.description: Owns casualty counts, hospital information, family reunification and the public message on protective actions.

roles.name: Operations Section Chief
roles.description: Owns tactics across suppression, rescue, EMS and hazmat branches, and the staging of arriving units.

roles.name: Fire Suppression Group Supervisor
roles.description: Owns attack, search, ventilation, water supply and accountability reports for the companies inside.

roles.name: Medical Group Supervisor (Medical Branch Director)
roles.description: Establishes the triage, treatment and patient transportation units (groups under a Medical Branch), sets the triage method, and owns hospital capacity and destination decisions.

roles.name: Patient Transportation Unit Leader (Group Supervisor under a Medical Branch)
roles.description: Owns ambulance staging and loading, the order patients leave in, destination assignment and air resources.

roles.name: Hazmat Group Supervisor
roles.description: Owns identification of the material, isolation and protective action recommendations, entry, decontamination and product control, at the responder level the team is trained to.

roles.name: Dispatcher (Telecommunicator)
roles.description: Owns unit assignment, tone-outs, mutual aid alerts, call load across the rest of the county and the radio channels.

roles.name: EMS Medical Director
roles.description: Advises on protocol deviations, triage and treatment policy during a mass casualty incident, and field termination of resuscitation.

roles.name: Healthcare Coalition Liaison
roles.description: Reports regional bed counts, diversion and patient tracking from the hospital side, and relays what the hospitals can take.

outsideParties: the 911 center and neighboring dispatch centers
receiving hospitals and the regional healthcare coalition
the American Red Cross and mass care providers
the county health department and public health
the chemical facility and its emergency coordinator
CHEMTREC and the shipper or carrier
the state fire marshal and the state emergency management agency
schools, venues and neighbors inside the protective action zone
mediaChannels: a bystander's video posted to social media within minutes
the local TV assignment desk and a news helicopter
a scanner stream with listener comments
a neighborhood app post from a resident near the plume
a family member's post asking where the injured were taken
a reporter's call to the PIO for the number of patients

sceneAnchors.public: bystanders held back behind yellow tape at a street intersection, ambulances and fire engines with their lights on, a paramedic kneeling beside a patient on a backboard, dusk
sceneAnchors.control: a mobile incident command post: a command vehicle with a whiteboard of unit assignments on a folding table, a chief in a white helmet with a radio, a map taped to the window
sceneAnchors.exterior: a roadway incident scene with fire engines and ambulances parked at angles, hose lines on the pavement, responders in turnout gear, a ladder truck at the edge of the frame, overcast sky

addedThreatFamilies.label: Mass casualty incident
addedThreatFamilies.description: A bus crash, explosion, collapse or crowd event produces more patients than the first units can treat, and triage, treatment, transport and hospital destinations decide who lives.

phaseArc.title: Dispatch and size-up
phaseArc.goal: The first units find more patients than they can handle and say so.
beats: the first unit gives a size-up with a patient count that is only a guess
the dispatcher sends the next alarm and tells the hospitals
the scene is not yet safe

phaseArc.title: MCI declaration, command and triage
phaseArc.goal: Command is established, the incident is declared an MCI, and triage starts with a named method.
beats: the incident commander declares an MCI and sets the triage method
the Medical Group and its triage, treatment and transportation units are filled by whoever is there
the tag count outruns the number of ambulances

phaseArc.title: Treatment, transport and destinations
phaseArc.goal: Patients leave in the right order for the right hospitals while hospital capacity changes.
beats: Immediate patients go first but the trauma center says it is full
a hospital reports diversion and the next ambulance is already loaded
an expectant patient's family arrives at the treatment area

phaseArc.title: Surge, reunification and demobilization
phaseArc.goal: Counts reconcile, families are told, and responders are released.
beats: the casualty count given to the media differs from the tag count
the family reunification center opens
critical incident stress and rehab for the crews

decisionPointExamples: send the next Immediate patient to the closer community hospital that can stabilize, or hold for the trauma center that has just reported diversion
keep treating an expectant patient or redirect the crew to a delayed patient who is deteriorating
declare the incident an MCI and activate the regional plan now, or wait for a second unit to confirm the count
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a revised patient count, a tag count that does not match the transport log, a hospital status change, a bystander who says more people were on the bus
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: ambulances stuck behind apparatus, a hospital that goes on diversion mid-transport, a radio channel overloaded with traffic, triage tags running out
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the Medical Communications Coordinator and the receiving hospitals through the healthcare coalition

decisionMustMention.description: the medical side: triage, treatment, transport, a hospital destination or a mutual aid request

addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: Name the triage method the players use in the first phase (START, SALT or the local method); the exercise does not pick one for them. Keep patient counts consistent between the CAD, the tags, the transport log and what the PIO says, unless an inject is meant to make them differ. Sequence transport with Immediate patients first and never abandon expectant patients. Use fictional patients with invented names and ages; no real patient data.

addedThreatFamilies.label: Hazardous materials release
addedThreatFamilies.description: A transportation or fixed-facility release forces responders to identify the material, set isolation and protective actions as the wind changes, decontaminate, and coordinate with the facility and the hospitals.

phaseArc.title: Call and identification
phaseArc.goal: Responders learn what is leaking from the placard, the shipping paper and the people who know.
beats: the caller reports a smell and a vapor cloud but no placard
the shipping papers are in a cab no one can reach
the first-arriving company stages upwind and uphill

phaseArc.title: Isolation and protective action
phaseArc.goal: The isolation zone and the downwind protective action are chosen, announced and then revisited as the wind moves.
beats: the incident commander chooses between shelter in place and evacuation for the downwind area
the wind shifts and the plume points at a school or care facility
the public message is ready after the first sirens

phaseArc.title: Entry, rescue and decontamination
phaseArc.goal: Entry teams work at their level of training, victims are decontaminated before they reach the ambulances, and the hospitals are warned.
beats: a technician team is needed but only operations-level crews are on scene
victims walk out of the warm zone before decontamination is set up
the hospital asks what the patients are contaminated with

phaseArc.title: Product control and recovery
phaseArc.goal: The leak is controlled, zones are reduced and the investigation begins.
beats: the carrier's contractor arrives
residents ask when they can go home
the facility's emergency coordinator asks for the exercise report

decisionPointExamples: order the downwind neighborhood to shelter in place, or evacuate it through a road that may cross the plume
extend the protective action zone as the wind shifts toward the elementary school, or hold the current lines and watch the monitors
send an entry team to attempt a rescue now, or wait for the technician team and accept the delay
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a placard number, a shipping paper line, a monitor reading, a wind observation, a victim's symptoms, a call from the facility's emergency coordinator
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: a wind shift, a blocked evacuation route, a meter that reads off scale, decontamination water supply, an entry team below the required level
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the facility's emergency coordinator, the shipper through CHEMTREC, and the receiving hospitals

decisionMustMention.description: an isolation or protective action, entry, decontamination or PPE choice

addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: Players are told to use their own copy of the Emergency Response Guidebook for real decisions. Never invent distances for a real UN number: use the isolation and protective action numbers the facilitator entered, or a fictional material with clearly labeled exercise distances. Keep players at their responder level: awareness, operations, technician, specialist or incident commander. The initial isolation zone is a circle; the protective action zone is a downwind square.

addedThreatFamilies.label: Structure fire and command transfer
addedThreatFamilies.description: A working fire escalates, a mayday is called, and command changes hands while accountability is kept.

phaseArc.title: Dispatch and size-up
phaseArc.goal: The first company sizes up the building and commits to an attack.
beats: the first officer gives a size-up and takes command
water supply is a long lay
a bystander says someone may be inside

phaseArc.title: Attack, accountability and mayday
phaseArc.goal: Companies work inside, and a firefighter's call for help tests accountability.
beats: conditions worsen and the incident commander orders a personnel accountability report
a firefighter calls a mayday
the rapid intervention team deploys

phaseArc.title: Command transfer and mutual aid
phaseArc.goal: Command passes to a higher-ranking officer with a briefing while mutual aid arrives.
beats: the battalion chief arrives and takes command
the old and new commanders disagree on the strategy
mutual aid companies need assignments and a radio channel

phaseArc.title: Overhaul and investigation
phaseArc.goal: The fire is out, the accountability review runs, and the investigation begins.
beats: the fire marshal asks to hold the scene
the accountability review shows a gap in the tag system
the PIO is asked about the injured firefighter

decisionPointExamples: go defensive and pull every company out, or commit another crew to a rescue that may already be lost
transfer command now with a hurried briefing, or finish the rescue first under the original commander
call for a personnel accountability report on the main channel and risk tying it up during a mayday
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a size-up report, an accountability tag count, a mayday radio message, a thermal image reading, a water supply status
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: a radio channel that is overloaded, a collapse warning, a hydrant that is out of service, an incoming company with the wrong equipment
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the dispatcher, the rapid intervention team, and the mutual aid companies

decisionMustMention.description: command, accountability, a mayday or a switch between offensive and defensive operations

addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: Stay at the coordination and decision level: who commands, who is accountable, what is announced on which channel and when. Do not write step-by-step fireground tactics or building-specific attack instructions. A command transfer always names who is giving command, who is taking it, the time, and the briefing.

addedThreatFamilies.label: Technical rescue
addedThreatFamilies.description: A trench, confined space, collapse or rope rescue where access, stabilization and a medical handoff are the hard parts.

phaseArc.title: Access and stabilization
phaseArc.goal: The scene is made safe enough to work in.
beats: the first unit reports a victim and an unstable structure or trench wall
bystanders have already tried to dig
the rescue team is paged

phaseArc.title: Rescue plan
phaseArc.goal: The team chooses an approach and a safety margin.
beats: the team leader proposes a plan and the safety officer objects
a utility line is in the way
the family arrives

phaseArc.title: Extrication
phaseArc.goal: The victim is reached while conditions change.
beats: a secondary collapse changes the plan
the air monitor reads low in the confined space
the medical unit stages for the handoff

phaseArc.title: Medical handoff
phaseArc.goal: The patient moves to the ambulance with a hand-off report.
beats: the patient is entrapped longer than expected
the hospital is told what to expect
the investigation begins

decisionPointExamples: continue the rescue under a wall the engineer has not cleared, or wait for shoring at a cost to the victim
send in a second rescuer after a monitor alarm, or hold until the space is ventilated
ask for the regional rescue team now or wait to see whether local resources can finish
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a shoring inspection, an air monitor reading, a utility locate, a bystander's account of how long the victim has been trapped
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: ground conditions, a utility strike, a long haul for equipment, a medical unit that cannot reach the staging point
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the structural or trench specialist and the utility owner

decisionMustMention.description: the rescue plan, stabilization, monitoring, entry or the safety officer

addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: Stay at the coordination and decision level. Do not write rescue techniques, load calculations or shoring dimensions.

addedThreatFamilies.label: Response system degradation
addedThreatFamilies.description: The systems that move responders fail or saturate: CAD or radio, a hospital diversion cascade, a staffing shortage, or several incidents at once.

phaseArc.title: First signs
phaseArc.goal: A small failure is noticed by the people who feel it first.
beats: units stop receiving CAD updates on their mobile terminals
a hospital goes on diversion
a second call comes in from across the county

phaseArc.title: Workaround
phaseArc.goal: Dispatch and responders fall back to voice and paper.
beats: run cards come out and the dispatcher works from the whiteboard
radio traffic jams the main channel
a unit is sent to the wrong address

phaseArc.title: Cascade
phaseArc.goal: Resources run short as more incidents arrive.
beats: the closest ambulance is committed and the next is twenty minutes away
the neighboring county cannot send mutual aid
diversion spreads to a second hospital

phaseArc.title: Recovery
phaseArc.goal: Systems return and the gaps are measured.
beats: CAD comes back with a backlog of unsynchronized records
response times are reviewed
the director faces the press

decisionPointExamples: pull a unit out of one district to cover a worse call in another, leaving the first uncovered
send the ambulance to a diverted hospital that is closer, or to an open one that is 25 minutes farther
request state resources now or wait for the neighboring county's answer
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a status board that stopped updating, an unanswered unit, a hospital status call, a call-load number
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: a radio channel that is saturated, a unit that is out of position, a whiteboard that does not match the real unit list
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the dispatch center and the healthcare coalition
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: The 911 center's own response to a CAD failure belongs to the emergency communications domain; here show what the responders and the dispatchers who send them see and decide.

noiseExamples: a car alarm that keeps going off down the block
a resident asking whether the smoke is from the fire
a unit radioing for a meal break during a quiet stretch
an unrelated lift-assist call from the other side of the county
a vendor calling about an apparatus delivery date
pressureExamples: a reporter on the line asking how many are dead before the count is known
a bystander video that shows a patient left on the ground
a council member asking why the neighboring department was not called sooner
a family member in the treatment area demanding to ride in the ambulance
a facility manager insisting there is no danger beyond the fence
